Infants
ĭn´fănts
n. pl. (the newly born and very young; in Scripture objects of Christ's welcome and of war's worst cruelty)
Latin infans, not speaking, from in- + fari, to speak. The Greek of Luke 18 is brephos, a babe in arms or unborn — the same word used of John leaping in Elisabeth's womb.

Biblical Definition

Job wishes he had been “as infants which never saw light” (Job 3:16). Hosea records the atrocity Samaria had earned: “their infants shall be dashed in pieces, and their women with child shall be ripped up” (Hos 13:16). And Luke sets against both the scene at which the disciples took offence: “they brought unto him also infants, that he would touch them: but when his disciples saw it, they rebuked them” (Luk 18:15) — and the Lord overruled them, “Suffer little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God” (Luk 18:16). The word Luke uses for these infants is the word he used of the unborn Baptist.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an infant as a child in the first period of life, and in law a person under the age of full legal capacity, entitled to particular protection.

expand to see more

INFANT, n. A child in the first period of life, beginning at his birth; a young babe.

INFANT, n. In law, a person under the age of twenty one years, who is incapable of making a valid contract.

INFANTILE, a. Pertaining to infancy, or to an infant.

Key Scripture

Job 3:16 — "Or as an hidden untimely birth I had not been; as infants which never saw light."

Hos 13:16 — "Samaria shall become desolate; for she hath rebelled against her God: they shall fall by the sword: their infants shall be dashed in pieces, and their women with child shall be ripped up."

Luk 18:15 — "And they brought unto him also infants, that he would touch them: but when his disciples saw it, they rebuked them."

Luk 18:16 — "But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Suffer little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God."

Modern Corruption

Luke uses the same word for the infants in arms and for the unborn John, and the child in the womb is therefore not a candidate for personhood but a person.

expand to see more

The vocabulary is decisive. Luke 1:41 says the brephos leaped in Elisabeth's womb; Luke 2:12 says the brephos lay in the manger; Luke 18:15 says they brought unto Him the brephos. One word covers the unborn, the newborn, and the babe in arms, because Scripture recognizes no boundary between them. Psalm 139 says the same in the language of worship — thou hast covered me in my mother's womb; mine substance was not hid from thee. Jeremiah 1:5 says it in the language of calling. The child in the womb is a human being made in the image of God, known by name before birth.

The corruption to name is the doctrine that personhood is conferred by development, viability, or the wishes of others, which is the argumentative core of abortion in every form it takes. It is not a new error but an ancient one wearing modern language: the exposure of unwanted infants was ordinary in the Greco-Roman world the church was born into, and the church opposed it from the beginning. Hosea 13:16 names the killing of infants as the extremity of judgment and horror, not as a private matter. And the answer of Christ to disciples who thought children beneath His time is the answer still: suffer them to come, and forbid them not.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek brephos (G1025), an unborn child, newborn, or babe in arms; paidion (G3813), little child; Hebrew olel (H5768), infant, suckling.

expand to see more

Greek brephos (G1025) — unborn child, babe; Luke 1:41, 2:12, 18:15, Acts 7:19.

Greek paidion (G3813) — little child; Luke 18:16, Matthew 18:2.

Hebrew olel (H5768) — infant, suckling; Hosea 13:16, Psalm 8:2, Lamentations 2:11.

Hebrew nephel (H5309) — untimely birth; Job 3:16, Ecclesiastes 6:3.

Hebrew yatsar (H3335) — to form, fashion; Jeremiah 1:5, Psalm 139:16.

Usage

"“They brought unto him also infants, that he would touch them” — and the disciples rebuked them."

"“Of such is the kingdom of God” — the Lord's correction."

"“As infants which never saw light” — Job in the depth of his grief."
